title: Social protection is being redesigned as productive, ecological, and digital infrastructure for household autonomy in climate-exposed Mozambique
source_unit: World Bank feature story, Roots of Resilience: How Mozambique's Families Are Rebuilding Their Lives and Their Land, published 18 September 2026
geography: Mozambique; Productive Social Action Program across all 11 provinces, with reported examples in Zambezia and Sofala

observations.period: 2012–2026; Productive Social Action Program reach and design

denominator.unit: Mozambicans who have participated in PASP since its launch

programme_bundle.value: cash or income support combined with skills development, productive grants, and community work

targeting.value: vulnerable, climate-exposed, and economically marginalized families, with women comprising most participants

observations.method: World Bank feature story summarizing PASP reach, design, implementation, and beneficiary accounts; it is not a randomized evaluation or representative household survey.
observations.uncertainty: The feature does not provide a complete beneficiary denominator, transfer adequacy, attrition, comparison group, or independently verified aggregate livelihood effects.
observations.subgroup: Poor and climate-exposed households, women, small farmers, caregivers, informal workers, rural communities, and families facing food and livelihood insecurity.
observations.counterinterpretation: Combining transfers and productive activities can increase administrative burden or condition support on work that excludes people with care, disability, or health constraints; participation counts do not prove durable autonomy.

observations.period: 2012–2026; gendered participation and household investment route

household_investment.value: reported uses include farming, small businesses, housing improvements, food, school materials, and children's futures

economic_pathway.value: income, skills, and productive grants are intended to support jobs, self-employment, assets, and livelihoods after programme support

observations.method: World Bank feature highlights programme composition and reported beneficiary uses of income and skills.
observations.uncertainty: The gender share and household uses are reported by the source; the feature does not establish whether investments are typical, sustained, or sufficient to change gendered bargaining power or poverty trajectories.
observations.subgroup: Women beneficiaries, caregivers, children, small-enterprise operators, farmers, and households allocating scarce income across food, housing, education, and productive assets.
observations.counterinterpretation: Women’s high participation can reflect gendered targeting and unpaid care burdens rather than equal economic power; household investment may trade off with consumption or care time.

public_work_types.value: coastal protection, riverbank restoration, erosion control, rural infrastructure, and landscape restoration

livelihood_link.value: participants receive income while developing practical skills and contributing to projects that protect farms, homes, and local ecosystems

household_resilience.value: the feature reports improved food security, more resilient housing, and productive assets among example households and communities

observations.method: World Bank narrative account linking social-protection participation to climate adaptation work and household examples.
observations.uncertainty: The source does not quantify avoided climate losses, asset durability, ecological impact, or whether public works create net additional employment or displace other local work.
observations.subgroup: Climate-exposed households, coastal and riverine communities, farmers, women, local authorities, ecosystems, and households whose homes or livelihoods face erosion and extreme weather.
observations.counterinterpretation: Public works can provide short-term income without changing structural exposure; ecological benefits may be localized, delayed, or vulnerable to larger shocks and maintenance gaps.

denominator.unit: electronic money accounts opened through PASP

payment_effect.value: mobile-money transfers reduce travel time, improve security, and provide easier access to funds

financial_inclusion.value: many participants accessed formal financial services for the first time

post_programme_examples.value: former beneficiaries are reported to continue farming, building stronger houses, producing for household consumption and local markets, and using acquired skills after support

observations.method: World Bank feature description of PASP payment infrastructure and selected post-programme household and community examples.
observations.uncertainty: Account opening is not active use, savings, or financial well-being; the post-programme examples are illustrative and do not establish population-level persistence or causal impact.
observations.subgroup: Remote and rural beneficiaries, women, caregivers, households with high travel costs, small producers, mobile-money users, and people newly entering formal finance.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital payments can create fees, fraud, exclusion, SIM or identity barriers, and new dependence on payment infrastructure; travel-time savings do not automatically become household leisure or care relief.

related_sources.claim: World Bank Social Protection for Economic Resilience Project associated with PASP.
World Bank country context for Mozambique.

boundary: This record adds a route from cash and social protection through skills, productive assets, ecological public work, mobile money, household room, and climate resilience. It is based on a World Bank feature story and beneficiary narratives, not a representative survey, randomized evaluation, complete programme administrative dataset, or proof of durable autonomy and ecological impact.
